title: AI Agents
text:
A chatbot answers, and you take the next step yourself: you copy the code, run it, paste back the error. An agent takes those steps on its own. Under the hood it is the same language model; the difference is what is built around it. A working definition: an LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal.
Everything else, the plan, the instructions it loads, the sub-agents, the context it keeps in mind, is built around that loop. This page answers:

What is the difference between a chatbot and an agent?
What are the parts of an agent, and what does each one do?
When is an agent the right choice, and when is a fixed workflow better?
Why are agents suddenly everywhere?
What can go wrong when an agent acts with your permissions?

title: AI Agents
text:
Explanation

The model, the tools, the loop
The language model can only produce text. It cannot open a file or load a web page. What it can do is write down which tool it wants to call, and with which arguments: read a file, write a file, run a command, search the web. A program on your computer executes the call and hands the result back to the model. Then the model decides what to do next. This loop, think, act, observe, repeats until the goal is reached. In research the pattern is known as ReAct (Yao et al., 2022).


Context, plans and sub-agents
Everything the agent “knows” during a task sits in its context window: the goal, every tool result, every intermediate thought. When it fills up, the agent has to summarise or forget. To stay on track, agents write themselves a plan, a to-do list they tick off, and read instructions stored in text files when they need them. For big tasks they can start sub-agents: copies of themselves, each with a fresh context window, working in parallel.


Workflow or agent?
Not everything with AI inside is an agent. A workflow follows predefined steps; an agent decides the next step itself. The advice from Anthropic: keep it as simple as possible, and use agents only where the task needs that freedom.


Handle with care
An agent acts with your permissions. It can read every file you can read, run every command you can run, and publish to the internet. Whoever gives an agent access hands over their own keys. Asking it to show its plan before it acts is where you stay in control.

title: A Brief History of AI
text:
When did artificial intelligence begin: in 1950 with Alan Turing, in 1956 at a workshop in Dartmouth, or in 2022 with ChatGPT? Instead of answering from a slide, we collect what you already know on a pinboard and hand it to an AI agent. The agent researches every milestone, reads the sources, checks last year’s list for errors, and turns the result into an interactive timeline with a quiz.
What the agent does along the way is the programme of this course:

How can a model read a photo of handwriting?
How does a language model write a plan, code and text?
Why does it use tools, and when are rules better than learning?
Can we trust facts an AI has checked?
What happens when an agent splits its work among sub-agents, or publishes on its own?

title: Overview
text:
This page will show the map of topics for this course: which concepts there are, how they build on each other, and where each one appears in the experiments. Until the map is ready, here are the concepts that already have a page of their own:

A Brief History of AI: seventy-five years of artificial intelligence, compiled live by an AI agent.
AI Agents: a language model that uses tools in a loop to reach a goal.

title: Artificial Intelligence
text:
Everybody talks about AI agents: programs that get a goal instead of a recipe, plan their own steps, use tools, and keep going until the job is done. You will watch one at work, try one yourself, and then open it up, layer by layer.
We start at the top, with the agent you have just seen in action, and work our way down: to the language model inside it, to how that model represents text and meaning, to how it was trained, and finally to the simple idea of learning from data. Then we climb back up and ask what all this means for your field and for the rest of us.
Every session starts with an experiment. You do something first and understand it afterwards, often with pen, paper and a table before any computer comes in. All experiments can be repeated at home. Where there is code to write, you don’t type it yourself: you tell an AI agent what you need and check what it builds.
